rashi:a1.1: And an item that is not appraised when alive: such as the hide and the sinews, since the importance of the appraisal of the animal’s value is not on account of the hide. Therefore, by means of inclusion it is permitted, even [the animal tithe] of an adult. And for orphans, because of [the principle of] returning a lost item, they kept it at Torah law, that after slaughter one sells it in its usual manner.
gershom:a1.1: An item that is not appraised when alive: that is, the hide, which is appraised only after death. The Rabbis did not decree after slaughter that it may not be sold by inclusion on account of before slaughter; rather, it is sold by inclusion.
gershom:a2.1: And with orphans the Rabbis kept it at Torah law: they did not decree about them, for the benefit of the orphans, but kept it at Torah law, that while alive it is not sold, but after slaughter it is sold even not by inclusion.
rashi:a2.1: He holds in accordance with that of Rava: that an animal tithe after slaughter is permitted to be sold by Torah law.
tosafot:a2.1: And even Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak holds in accordance with that of Rava: that is, from another verse, and not for his reason.
rashi:a3.1: Notwithstanding, after all the desire of your soul: in the Sifrei we establish that it speaks of disqualified consecrated animals, and it is written “you may slaughter and eat.”
rashi:a3.2: Which is the item that has no blessing when alive: that one may not derive benefit from them while alive; for other consecrated animals, if a blemish befell them, one redeems them and may sell them while alive to whomever he wishes.
rashi:a3.3: Rather, this is the animal tithe: of which it is written “it shall not be redeemed,” that it is not sold while alive; and it is written that after slaughter there is a blessing. And that blessing is selling, for, parallel to the blessing that He prohibited to you while alive, He permitted to you after slaughter; and what blessing would have been fitting for it while alive? Selling. Evidently, after slaughter it is sold by Torah law, and that which is taught, “it is not sold slaughtered,” is rabbinic. Therefore, for orphans we keep it at Torah law.
gershom:a3.1: Which is the item that has no blessing when alive: that is, while alive it is prohibited to sell it and to derive benefit from it, but after slaughter it is permitted. You must say: the animal tithe of orphans. For if of an adult, the Rabbis decreed about it after slaughter on account of before slaughter. And if other disqualified consecrated animals, even while alive they are sold after their redemption. [The printed edition adds a note: It appears from Rabbeinu’s wording that he read in the Gemara “this is the animal tithe of orphans.” This is not understood, since for adults too it is permitted by Torah law to sell after slaughter, and this Amora is speaking of the verse; this requires further study.]
rashi:a4.1: What is it to include: the value of the meat of the animal tithe of an adult together with the value of the bones.
gershom:a4.1: In its bones: [to include] the meat in the value of the bones.
rashi:a5.1: A small animal: the bones are not fit for anything, and one does not include.
rashi:a5.2: A large animal: the bones are fit for handles of carpenters’ tools and of axes, and one includes.
gershom:a5.1: This is with a large animal: its bones are valuable for craftwork, and one may include [the meat] in them.
rashi:a6.1: In the locale of this Sage: they make utensils from bones; and in the locale of that Sage they do not make utensils from bones, and one does not include.
gershom:a6.1: Each Sage according to his locale: the one who says one includes [lived where] bones are valued, for they make flutes from them; and in the locale of the Sage who says one does not include, they do not make flutes from them.
rashi:a7.1: From where are these matters derived: that an animal tithe is not sold; for how does “it shall not be redeemed” imply selling?
rashi:a8.1: With regard to dedications: it is written (Leviticus 27:28): “It may neither be sold nor redeemed; every dedicated item is most holy,” etc.
rashi:a9.1: Free: for these words “it shall not be redeemed” must be free for this exposition.
rashi:a9.2: In that they apply to all: for if one declared consecrated items to be dedications, the dedication takes effect on them, and he gives the priest according to the benefit of discretion that he has in them, as it says in Arakhin, in the chapter HaMakdish Sadehu (Arakhin 28b). Would you say the same of the tithe, which takes effect only on non-sacred animals? And furthermore, a dedication takes effect on the entire herd, while the tithe is only the tenth.
gershom:a7.1: In that they apply to all: whether to offerings of the most sacred order, to offerings of lesser sanctity, or to non-sacred property. The animal tithe takes effect only on non-sacred animals.
tosafot:a10.1: Let the verse not state “it shall not be redeemed” with regard to dedications, and derive it from the tithe: just as the tithe is sacred and not redeemed. And if you say: perhaps we would derive it from [ordinary] consecrated property, which is redeemed? One can say that we derive toward stringency. Alternatively, because with regard to dedications it is written “it may not be sold,” we would apply “it shall not be redeemed” to them as well.
gershom:a8.1: So too dedications are sacred: as it is written, “Every dedicated item is most holy.”
gershom:a9.1: To be free, and to derive the tithe from it: just as “it shall not be redeemed” of dedications [comes with] “it shall not be sold” too, so too “it shall not be redeemed” of the tithe [means] “it shall not be sold” too.
rashi:a11.1: It can be refuted: so that “it shall not be redeemed” of dedications is needed, since we cannot learn it from the tithe: what is notable about the tithe, that it is sacred before it and after it? For if he called the tenth “ninth,” and the ninth “tenth,” and the eleventh “tenth,” all three are consecrated.
gershom:a10.1: In that it sanctifies before it and after it: as we learned: if he called the ninth “tenth,” and the tenth “tenth,” and the eleventh “tenth,” all three are consecrated. This is not so with dedications.
rashi:a13.1: For it can be refuted: with regard to the tithe, as we refuted regarding dedications: what is notable about the firstborn, that its sanctity is from the womb? Would you say the same of the tithe, whose sanctity is not from the womb? And that is why “it shall not be redeemed” of the tithe is needed.
gershom:a11.1: It can be refuted as we refuted: what is notable about the firstborn, that its sanctity is from the womb?
rashi:a16.1: And “you shall cause to pass” is a superfluous verse: and it is free for a verbal analogy, to teach “passing” and “passing” for the tithe, that it shall not be redeemed, and one does not refute it. Therefore “it shall not be redeemed” of the tithe is free. And why is this verse superfluous? Because it could have written “all that opens the womb is the Lord’s,” as another verse writes (Exodus 13), “all that opens the womb is Mine.” Why do I need “and you shall cause to pass”? Conclude from it that it is a superfluous verse.
gershom:a12.1: And “you shall cause to pass” is superfluous: that is, the verse did not need to say “and you shall cause to pass,” for it could have said “and you shall give all that opens the womb.” Rather, why was it written in the language of “you shall cause to pass”? For the comparison, and one does not refute a comparison; and that leaves “it shall not be redeemed” free in the tithe, to learn from “it shall not be redeemed” of dedications: just as there selling is with it, so too here selling is with it. One cannot say that the “passing” of the tithe is superfluous, since the tithe is learned from the firstborn.
rashi:a17.1: Let us derive the firstborn too, redemption and redemption from dedications: that it may not be sold; for although “redemption” [geula] is not written with regard to the firstborn, “redemption” [pediya] is written with regard to it (ibid.), and it is the same thing.
rashi:a17.2: Redemption of the tithe is free: as we said; therefore we judge it by a verbal analogy from dedications. But the pediya of the firstborn is not free, since it is needed for itself and also to teach the tithe through “passing” and “passing.”
gershom:a13.1: Let us derive the firstborn too, redemption: from dedications, and let it not be sold. [Answer:] That of the tithe is free, etc. And let us derive the firstborn, that it not be sold, “passing” and “passing” from the tithe, for we have found that the tithe is prohibited to be sold, since it is derived “redemption” and “redemption” from dedications; let the firstborn be derived from the tithe. [Answer:] “It,” as it is written “most holy it is,” as it is written “every dedicated item is most holy it is.”
rashi:a18.1: And what did you see: that the pediya of the firstborn is for itself and to teach the tithe, and “it shall not be redeemed” of the tithe is to be free and to derive a verbal analogy from dedications? Say instead that “it shall not be redeemed” of the tithe is for itself, that it is not redeemed, and to teach the firstborn through “passing” and “passing,” and that of the firstborn is to be free and to derive a verbal analogy from dedications, that it is prohibited to be sold.
rashi:a22.1: And let us derive the firstborn, passing, from the tithe: that it be prohibited to be sold, for regarding the tithe we have already established that we derive it, redemption [and redemption], from dedications.
tosafot:a23.1: “It,” and not the firstborn: Rava too, who answers below that “it shall not be sold” with regard to dedications is not needed, also holds “it, and not the firstborn,” as is evident in the first chapter of Temura (5b), regarding “if one does it, it is not effective”; for were it not for “it,” we would derive the firstborn, “passing” and “passing,” from the tithe. And Abaye too, who establishes “it” in the first chapter of Temura as “it shall remain in its being,” nevertheless would expound “it, and not the firstborn,” since “it” is juxtaposed to “most holy,” which implies: it shall remain in its sanctity.
rashi:a23.1: It stands to reason, the tithe: should be included in the law of dedications, since “redemption” [geula] is written with regard to it as with dedications; and the firstborn should be excluded, since pediya is written with regard to it.
rashi:a24.1: “It shall not be redeemed” of dedications is not needed: and not because it is derived from the firstborn, but rather we know by reasoning that it is not subject to redemption.
tosafot:a24.1: Rava says: “It shall not be redeemed” of dedications is not needed: so it is written in the books, but Rashi reads “it shall not be sold,” because he infers [from the Gemara’s words] “where are they? If with the owner, they are consecrated”; and if it were speaking of “it shall not be redeemed,” surely items consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed! And Rabbeinu Tam explains that “they are consecrated” means even if they were redeemed, for “most holy” implies to him intrinsic sanctity until it comes into the priest’s hand. However, it is difficult for the Ri [our teacher]: in the first chapter of Temura (5b) it is implied that we prove that redemption is not effective from “it shall remain in its being,” according to Abaye, who says that if one does it, it is effective; and according to Rava, who says it is not effective, it is derived from “it shall not be redeemed” itself. If so, how could he infer here that “it shall not be redeemed” is not needed because with the owner they are consecrated even if they were redeemed? Rava derives that very thing from “it shall not be redeemed”! And there is another difficulty, which Rashi raised: what he says, “If it is not relevant to dedications, apply it to the tithe” — why does the tithe need the “it shall not be redeemed” of dedications, when it is written of the tithe itself? And if it is because of “it shall not be sold,” in the sense of acquisition, he should have said this: “If it is not relevant to redemption, which is written of it itself, apply it to selling.” Alternatively, he should have said: “Why do I need ‘it shall not be redeemed’ of dedications? Conclude from it that it is to be free.”
gershom:a14.1: “It shall not be redeemed” of dedications is not needed: and you do not need to derive it from a verbal analogy. For where are the dedications? If with the owner, they are consecrated, and it is prohibited to redeem unblemished consecrated animals.
rashi:a24.2: They are consecrated: and are not subject to redemption, and they are not like offerings consecrated for the altar.
rashi:a24.3: They are non-sacred: and the priest may sell them to whomever he wishes.
rashi:a25.1: Every dedicated item is most holy, it: it is prohibited to be sold.
rashi:a25.2: Shall be yours: they are in the priest’s domain, like the rest of his property.
gershom:a15.1: If he gave them to the priest, they are like non-sacred property: and they are sold in the usual manner.
rashi:b1.1: Apply it to the matter of the tithe: for selling.
gershom:b1.1: Apply it to the matter of the tithe: this superfluous “it shall not be redeemed,” and for selling.
rashi:b1.2: It stands to reason that we apply it to the tithe, since redemption [geula] is written with regard to it as well. So I have heard. But I have much to reply. First, that he says, “If with the owner, they are consecrated” — but consecrated property is subject to redemption, for items consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed like items consecrated for the altar, as it is written, “And if the one who consecrated it will redeem his house”; so you are forced to say that it was necessary to write “it shall not be redeemed” with regard to dedications. And further, that he says, “Apply it to the matter of the tithe” — why must we bring “it shall not be redeemed” to the tithe, when “it shall not be redeemed” is already stated with regard to it? And if he means it for selling, he should have said further, “If it is not relevant to redemption, apply it to selling.” Alternatively, he should have said, “Why do I need ‘it shall not be redeemed’ of dedications? Conclude from it that it is to be free, and to derive a verbal analogy: just as here selling is with it, so too with the tithe selling is with it.” Therefore it seems to me that you must read it this way: Rava says, “‘It shall not be sold’ of dedications is not needed.” And this is its explanation: Rava says that we derive without a verbal analogy that the tithe is not sold, since “it shall not be sold” of dedications is not needed. [If they are with the owner,] they are consecrated, and with consecrated property the owner has no authority to sell it to others; rather, it is handed over to the Temple treasurer. And so too here, as long as they are in the owner’s possession they are not sold; [in the priest’s possession,] they are non-sacred and are sold. Apply it to the matter of the tithe, that it shall not be sold. And this is the main [reading].
rashi:b2.1: From where do I say it: since it prohibited it only while alive; for if it were redemption by the owner specifically, one would infer that after slaughter it is redeemed and its sanctity is transferred to its money.
gershom:b2.1: But this requires standing and valuation: before it is redeemed, and it is impossible to stand them up, since it has already been slaughtered. Rather, conclude from it that it means “it shall not be sold.”
rashi:b3.1: It requires standing and valuation; rather: certainly it is not subject to the law of redemption at all, and it is not sacred [enough] to transfer its sanctity to its money. And this “it shall not be redeemed” is “it shall not be sold,” and it is because one performs with it an act of the non-sacred that the Merciful One prohibited it. Therefore, while alive, when its sanctity is strong, it is prohibited; after slaughter, when its sanctity has weakened, since it is slaughtered outside [the Temple] to be eaten by non-priests, it is permitted to sell.
tosafot:b3.1: But after slaughter it is redeemed; but it requires standing and valuation: It is puzzling: let him establish it as a case where it is still convulsing, for it is like a living animal in all respects, as it says in the second chapter of Chullin (30a): “Was the money of the paschal offering rejected? But it is taught: If one slaughtered in it both organs or most of both,” etc. One can say that perhaps this would be considered like a living animal also with regard to substitution. And the Rav Rabbi Shimon of Joinville, of blessed memory, would explain that here, where the slaughter was completed properly, a convulsing animal is not considered like a living one. And I explained it all in [the chapter] Merubeh (Bava Kamma 76a), in the discussion of the cow that imparts the impurity of food.
gershom:b3.1: This works out well according to the one who says altar offerings were included: in the mitzva of standing and valuation. You said [so], since it is not resolved with “it shall not be redeemed” literally.
gershom:b4.1: But according to the one who says, etc.: Rav Ashi would say to you: this is what we said. That is, from this we infer that it means “it shall not be sold”: for is there anything that, while alive, when it is strong enough to transfer its sanctity to its redemption, is not redeemed, and after slaughter, when it is not strong, is redeemed? Rather, conclude from it that this “it shall not be redeemed” is “it shall not be sold.”
rashi:b8.1: Redemption implies [redemption] by the owner, with its redemption money taking on its sanctity; for if its redemption money did not take on its sanctity, why would its owner redeem it? Rather, conclude from it [that it means] “it shall not be sold”: the verse prohibited it because of acts of the non-sacred.
rashi:b8.2: That is why it wrote “it shall not be redeemed”: since it expressed selling in the language of redemption, conclude from it that it may not be sold and may not be redeemed. And it cannot be established as redemption alone, for if so we could not infer that after slaughter it is redeemed.
rashi:b9.1: Mishna. He shall not be counted: even if a priest invited an Israelite guest to [partake of] the blemished firstborn, he may not eat with him.
gershom:b5.1: An Israelite shall not be counted with the priest: on a blemished firstborn, to eat it with him.
rashi:b10.1: Gemara. The mishna: which permits a gentile to eat the firstborn.
rashi:b10.2: Whose is it? It is Rabbi Akiva’s: who permits [it], and he says it according to Beit Hillel: Rabbi Akiva says that Beit Hillel permit even a gentile.
tosafot:b10.1: In brief: Ruling. The Ri says the halakha follows Beit Hillel of the mishna, who permit even a gentile, and not Beit Hillel of the baraita, who prohibit and disagree with Rabbi Akiva: where there is an unattributed mishna and a dispute in a baraita, the halakha follows the unattributed mishna (Yevamot 42b), all the more so here, where the mishna is unattributed in the very wording of the baraita, which is stronger than other unattributed rulings (Shabbat 157a). Tosafot then discusses the reason given below for Rabbi Akiva, “as the gazelle and as the deer,” and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar’s derivation (Chullin 28a): this implies that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], that birds require slaughter by Torah law, and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina (Nazir 29a) is no proof otherwise; alternatively, Rabbi Akiva may hold like Rabbi Elazar HaKappar and derive one point from the gazelle and one from the deer (see 15a). Halakhot Gedolot seems to rule like Beit Hillel of the baraita, the meat being prohibited to a gentile only by rabbinic law, while the fat is permitted since disqualified consecrated animals are compared to the gazelle and deer. There is no proof of a prohibition for gentiles from “you may eat, and not your dogs” (Pesachim 29a), nor from the unattributed rulings that a blemished firstborn must be buried (21b, 28a, 37a; Chullin 69b): those concern a firstborn prohibited to an Israelite as well, which is not compared to the gazelle and deer, as even Rabbi Akiva agrees (Zevachim 103b–104a; see 14a). Tosafot discusses at length whether such meat and hide are buried or burned (the reading in Zevachim, Rashi there, the baraita of two sin offerings below on 33a with Temura 24a), suggesting distinctions between Temple times and nowadays; and asks from Orla 3:3 (Temura 34a), where a garment woven of firstborn wool is burned, answering that hair decays and burial suffices, while a garment might be dug up and used, or that the mishna there follows Rabbi Yehuda, who allows one to be stringent and burn what is to be buried. It also cites a Tosefta about wool plucked from an unblemished firstborn. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b11.1: Just as with the breast and thigh, priests yes, Israelites no: as it is written, “You, and your sons, and your daughters with you.”
